spoken: On the 7th of May 1943, Allied troops entered Tunis. Six months of German and Italian occupation were over.
One week later, Tunisia's ruler, Moncef Bey, was flown into exile, not by the Germans, but by the French.
To see why, we must go back through those six months, when four powers stood over Tunisia at once.
This is the story of its rulers, its nationalists, the persecuted, and those who helped them.
Since 1881, Tunisia had been a French protectorate. Its monarch, the Bey of Tunis, signed the laws.
But the real power lay with a French official, the resident general.
From 1940, the resident general was Admiral Jean-Pierre Esteva. He answered to Marshal Pétain's regime at Vichy, which worked with Nazi Germany.
In June 1942, Moncef Bey came to the throne. He asked Vichy for reforms, such as more Tunisians in government.
Then, on the 8th of November, the Allies landed in Morocco and Algeria, and the next day German aircraft landed outside Tunis.
Under pressure from Vichy, Esteva let them use French bases. German and Italian troops poured into Tunis, Bizerte and the east.
French troops in the west joined the Allies, and the front line cut Tunisia in two.
In occupied Tunis, the Bey and Vichy's admiral stayed in place, alongside the German and Italian commands.
The Bey refused an Italian offer to break with France and an American appeal to join the Allies, siding with neither camp.
For Muslims, Jews and Europeans alike, the occupation brought air raids, shortages and fear.
German propaganda tried to win over the Muslim majority. And the occupiers singled out the Jews.
About 90,000 Jews lived in Tunisia. Most were subjects of the Bey, like their Muslim neighbours.
Vichy's anti-Jewish laws applied from 1940, but the US Holocaust Memorial Museum says Esteva and both Beys stalled them.
And Italy shielded the Jews who held Italian citizenship.
With the German army came an SS unit under Walter Rauff, who had developed gas vans to murder Jews in eastern Europe.
Within two weeks, the Germans had arrested leaders of the Jewish community.
On the 6th of December, Rauff ordered the community to hand over men for forced labour, 2,000 at first, and then 3,000.
On the 9th of December, the SS broke into synagogues and rounded up Jewish men in the streets of Tunis.
Under threat, the community's own leaders had to draw up the lists of workers.
Its head, Paul Ghez, kept a diary. He called it Six Months under the Boot.
About 5,000 men were sent to forced labour, in 32 to about 40 camps, many near the front.
Yad Vashem writes that tens died in the worst camps, at Bizerte and Mateur, of disease, labour, punishment and bombing.
Gilbert Mazouz, aged 19, was shot by a German soldier on his way to a camp.
On the 22nd of December, the Germans levied 20 million francs on the community, blaming it for the Allied bombing.
Homes were seized and hostages taken, and in some towns Jews had to wear a yellow star.
A handful were deported to camps in occupied Poland.
Yad Vashem writes that the SS came prepared for far worse. Tunisia's Jews were saved because the Germans ran out of time.
Many Tunisians wanted independence from France. Their leading party was the Neo-Destour, led by a lawyer, Habib Bourguiba.
After protests in 1938, the French jailed him, and from 1940 they held him in a fort in Marseille.
In August 1942, he wrote from his cell to his party that Germany would not win the war, and could not win it.
He told them to work with de Gaulle's Free French.
Late in 1942, the Germans freed him and handed him to their Italian allies.
In January 1943, Rome received him with honours and wanted him to speak for the Axis. He would not.
Some Tunisian activists did work with the occupiers.
Brought back to Tunis in April 1943, Bourguiba told his party to back the Allies.
Some people helped. The historian Robert Satloff gathered their stories, and stories of betrayal too.
He tells of Moncef Bey's ministers, who warned Jewish leaders of German plans and pleaded for hostages.
And of Si Ali Sakkat, a former mayor of Tunis, who sheltered about 60 escaped workers on his farm near Zagwan.
On the coast, in Mahdia, German soldiers took over the house of a Jewish family, the Bookrees.
Khalid Abdul-Wahab, from a prominent Muslim family, dealt with the Germans on the town's behalf.
Anny Bookrees, then 11, later said he had learned that a German officer planned to assault her mother.
By night, he drove her family and the Ouzzans, about two dozen people, to his farm at Tlelsa.
They stayed some four months, until the British arrived in April 1943.
In 2007, Satloff nominated him to Yad Vashem, Israel's Holocaust memorial, as a Righteous Among the Nations.
The title has four tests. One of them is risk to the rescuer's life, liberty or position.
Yad Vashem's Commission found that he broke no law, and that the Germans knew the families were on the farm.
One woman sheltered there recalled putting on her yellow badge to be counted when soldiers came to check.
So, it ruled, in the absence of risk, he was not eligible, though it praised his solidarity.
Others disagree. Eva Weisel, sheltered there as a girl, recalled drunken German officers threatening the families.
So do his family and Satloff. The shelter is well attested. Whether it carried risk is disputed.
On the 7th of May 1943, British troops entered Tunis and Americans entered Bizerte. The forced labourers came home.
On the 13th of May, the last Axis armies in Africa surrendered. Esteva, flown to France by the Germans, was later convicted of treason.
The French authorities in Algiers, under General Henri Giraud, then accused Moncef Bey of collaborating with the Axis.
On the 14th of May, after he refused to abdicate, Giraud deposed him, and a plane took him to Laghouat, in Algeria.
General Alphonse Juin, who carried it out, later wrote that he had found nothing serious against him.
For Tunisia's Jews, Vichy's anti-Jewish laws stayed in force until 1944.
And the French closed the schools and newspapers of Tunisia's Italians.
Bourguiba, who had refused the Axis, was not charged. An American diplomat spoke up for him.
Many Tunisians saw the deposed Bey as a symbol, and his successor, Lameen Bey, as a usurper.
Moncef Bey died in exile in Pau, in France, in 1948. Thousands, Jews among them, followed his funeral in Tunis.
Bourguiba took Tunisia's cause abroad, and to prison again. In 1954, France promised self-rule.
On the 20th of March 1956, Tunisia became independent. In 1957, the monarchy was abolished, and Bourguiba became president.
Six months of occupation left many stories, each to be told on its own terms.
Tunisia's Jews lived through forced labour, fines and fear, and some did not come back.
Muslim and European families lived through air raids and shortages.
A Bey protected his subjects where he could, and lost his throne to the French.
Nationalists had to choose a side. Neighbours helped, and some betrayed.
The Tunis roundup is still commemorated, in Paris and in Tunis, and in La Marsa a square now bears Moncef Bey's name.
Some of this history is documented, and some is still disputed. Telling the two apart is part of remembering it.
